captions: Hello, and welcome to Atomic English, Stage 6. In this lesson: Breaking news.
Use the present perfect for news and recognise the features of a news article.
Here are some new words. Breaking news. News about something that has just happened. Journalist.
A person who writes news for newspapers, ti vi or websites. Source. Where information comes from.
And some more words. Interview. A meeting where someone answers questions. According to.
As reported by someone. Emergency. A sudden, serious and dangerous situation.
Time for a question. The video will stop. Which word means: news about something that has just happened?
Now some grammar: Present perfect for news.
News often begins with the present perfect to give the main fact, then uses the past simple for details.
For example: A storm has hit the coast. It arrived at 6 a.m.
For example: Scientists have found a new species of frog.
Now listen, and read along. Storm hits coastal town.
Storm Causes Flooding in Port Alba A powerful storm has hit the coastal town of Port Alba,
causing flooding in more than two hundred homes. The storm arrived at around 6 a.m.
on Tuesday, bringing winds of over 120 kilometres an hour.
Several trees fell onto roads, and the town's main bridge was closed for safety.
According to the fire service, no one has been seriously hurt.
‘Our emergency teams worked through the night,’ said Chief Officer Maria Santos in an interview.
Schools in the area will stay closed until Friday.
Residents have been asked to avoid the beach while the sea is still rough.
Another question. The video will stop. Where did the storm hit?
Well done! Today you learned new words, like breaking news, journalist, source.
You practised present perfect for news. And you read Storm hits coastal town.
Now try the practice questions. See you next time!

captions: Hello, and welcome to Atomic English, Stage 6. In this lesson: Ask the right questions.
Report questions and decide if a source is reliable.
Here are some new words. Reliable. That you can trust. Fake. Not real or true, made to trick people. Check.
Make sure something is correct.
And some more words. Share. Send something to other people, often on lai. Website.
A group of pages on the internet. Evidence. Facts that show something is true.
Time for a question. The video will stop. Which word means: that you can trust?
Now some grammar: Reported questions.
In reported questions the word order is like a statement (subject plus verb).
Use if, whether for yes or no questions. Move the tense back.
For example: ‘Where do you live?’ becomes She asked where I lived.
For example: ‘Is it true?’ becomes He asked if it was true.
Now listen, and read along. Is it real? Five questions to ask. Every day we see hundreds of stories on lai.
Some are true, but some are fake. How can you tell?
Last week our class interviewed Mr Lee, a news journalist. We asked him how he checked his stories.
He said that he always asked five questions. 1. Who wrote it? A reliable source tells you who the writer is.
2. When was it written? Old news is sometimes shared as if it were new. 3. Is there evidence?
Look for facts, numbers and quotes from real people.
4. Do other trusted websites report the same story? 5. How does it make me feel?
Fake stories often try to make you angry or scared, so that you share them quickly.
Mr Lee said that if we weren't sure, we shouldn't share the story.
Another question. The video will stop. Who did the class interview?
Well done! Today you learned new words, like reliable, fake, check. You practised reported questions.
And you read Is it real? Five questions to ask. Now try the practice questions. See you next time!

Every day we see hundreds of stories online. Some are true, but some are fake. How can you tell?
Last week our class interviewed Mr Lee, a news journalist. We asked him how he checked his stories. He said that he always asked five questions.
1. Who wrote it? A reliable source tells you who the writer is.
2. When was it written? Old news is sometimes shared as if it were new.
3. Is there evidence? Look for facts, numbers and quotes from real people.
4. Do other trusted websites report the same story?
5. How does it make me feel? Fake stories often try to make you angry or scared, so that you share them quickly.
Mr Lee said that if we weren't sure, we shouldn't share the story.
